\caption{(a) Relative count error $(\hat c-k)/k$ against requested repetitions

\subsection{Models undercount repetitions, proportionally}

Figure~\ref{fig:main}(a) shows the relative count error against $k$. Below
$k\!=\!6$ every model is essentially exact; above it, repeated items are rendered
with a median error of \ErrRepCk{}\% per checkpoint, or \ErrRep{}\%
$[\ErrRepLo{},\ErrRepHi{}]$ pooling items ($n=\ErrRepN{}$) --- pooling weights
checkpoints by surviving item count, so we quote both. Either way it is
one-directional: models produce \emph{fewer} repetitions than requested.

Within $k\le32$ that deficit is \emph{proportional}, not saturating --- not what
Theorem~\ref{thm:collapse}(iv) predicts. A constant fits the panel's median count
above $k\!=\!6$ with residual sum of squares \ShapeSatSSE{} against
\ShapePropSSE{} for $\hat c=\ShapePropSlope{}k$ (S10): the count tracks the
request, so no horizon lies inside this ladder.

\subsection{Past the ladder, the count does level off}

So we extended it, post hoc, to $k\in\{48,64,96,128\}$ on the \HzNModels{}
checkpoints that admit utterances that long: \HzModelNames{}. XTTS-v2's
$602$-mel-token ceiling ($\approx\!26$\,s) censors every $k\ge48$ item (S10). Tracking stops: the
repeated median sits at \HzMedRepKLo{} and \HzMedRepKHi{} at $k\!=\!48$ and
$128$ while the control climbs \HzMedCtlKLo{} to \HzMedCtlKHi{}. Of \HzNGen{}
generations \HzExclCap{} hit our budget and \HzExclDegen{} were degenerate,
leaving \HzNCellLo{}--\HzNCellHi{} per cell; dropping truncated items is
conservative, their counts being censored downward.

The controls stop us reading this as counting collapse alone: they saturate too,
so these decoders have a general utterance-length ceiling and the reportable
quantity is the \emph{ratio}, which divides it out. Fitting $\hat c(k)=\hat
K(1-e^{-k/\hat K})$ over the combined ladder --- $\hat K$ a saturation scale read
off counts, \emph{not} the theorem's $N^\ast$, a function of the unmeasured $q$
--- gives $\hat K_{\mathrm{rep}}=\HzNRep{}$ $[\HzNRepLo{},\HzNRepHi{}]$ against
$\hat K_{\mathrm{ctl}}=\HzNCtl{}$ $[\HzNCtlLo{},\HzNCtlHi{}]$: repetition
lowers the counting horizon \HzRatio{}-fold, saturating just past where our
ladder stopped, which is why $k\le32$ looked proportional.

The panel is not unanimous, and the exception is informative: intervals are
disjoint for \HzSepNames{}, while \HzRevNames{} shows \emph{no} repeated-side
saturation within $k\le128$ and inverts the ratio --- the same checkpoint that
shows no deficit at $k\le32$, a conditional theorem behaving conditionally.

What degrades with $k$ is reliability, not proportion: the exactly-right share
falls from \ExactRepKLo{}\% to \ExactRepKHi{}\% between
$k\!=\!\ExactRepKLoVal{}$ and $\ExactRepKHiVal{}$, for word, sentence and
place-value units alike. Because the claim is about models rather than our corpus, the checkpoint is the
unit of replication, each reduced to its own repeated-minus-control difference. The exactly-correct rate favours the control in all \CkExactN{} (mean
\CkExact{} points $[\CkExactLo{},\CkExactHi{}]$); the median-error gap is
positive in \CkErrNPos{} of \CkErrN{}, zero in \ErrBestModel{}. Those six
cluster into \FamExactN{} families, so the effective replicate count is nearer
\FamExactN{}: per family the exact-rate gap is \FamExact{} points, range
$[\FamExactLo{},\FamExactHi{}]$, positive in all \FamExactN{}. At either level
the panel is too small for significance testing --- the exact signed-rank floor
at $n\!=\!6$ is $0.031$ and no multiplicity correction clears $0.05$ (S11) --- so
we rest on effect sizes and their consistency.

\subsection{The limit is periodicity, not length}

Figure~\ref{fig:main}(a) is also the paper's sharpest test. Each control has its
twin's carrier and word count, differing only in that the $k$ copies of one word
become non-adjacent ones. Were the failure about length, attention span or
exposure bias, the curves would coincide. They do not: at $k\ge6$ the median
control error is \ErrCtl{}\% $[\ErrCtlLo{}, \ErrCtlHi{}]$ ($n=\ErrCtlN{}$), at
every $k$ up to $32$ and for every model. The contrast is sharpest
in exactly-correct renderings --- \ExactCtl{}\% for controls against
\ExactRep{}\% for their twins: decoders that miscount a repeated sequence five
times in six render its non-adjacent twin correctly nineteen times in twenty. Controls are not perfect --- the residual \CtlMissPct{}\% carry
genuine truncations --- but they are exact where the repeated items are not.

A caveat belongs here, not in a limitation list: above $k\!=\!8$ the control's
fillers cycle a pool of eight, making that contrast period-$1$ against
period-$8$. Where controls carry no repetition at all --- $k\le8$, and the
extension ladder's never-cycled $146$-word pool --- it survives: \ApLoRep{}\%
against \ApLoCtl{}\% exact at $k\le8$, median error \ApHiMedRep{} against
\ApHiMedCtl{} at $k\ge48$. Two further rivals, improbability and an acoustic
attractor, fail their own predictions (S8).

A fourth rival is architectural, the one the title stakes: perhaps any
synthesiser mishandles long repeated text. We ran the same ladder through
VITS~\cite{kim2021vits}, which has no autoregressive decoder --- a duration
predictor and flow vocoder emit the waveform in one shot, leaving
Assumption~\ref{ass:periodic} no recurrence to act on. It shows \emph{no}
dissociation: \NonARRep{}\% of repeated items exact against
\NonARCtl{}\% of controls, a gap of \NonARGap{} points where the panel's is
$+\ARPoolGap{}$, and all \NonARAbove{} AR checkpoints separate from it. VITS
degrades with length, on both families alike. This also settles what auditing the
recogniser could not: were blank-collapse manufacturing the gap, it would have
depressed VITS's repeated items too, same judge, same strings. VITS is smaller
than the panel, so only the within-model dissociation is compared.

\subsection{The decoder buys states more slowly under repetition}

Theorem~\ref{thm:collapse}(ii) says states visited under periodic conditioning
stop being mutually distinguishable, so more repetitions should buy distinct
internal states more slowly than non-repetitive text of the same length does. We
count states by the effective rank $\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{eff}}$ of the trajectory
and report the \emph{capacity gain}
$\mathrm{d}\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{eff}}/\mathrm{d}\log k$
(Figure~\ref{fig:main}(c)). On repeated text it is a factor \CapRatio{} of the
control gain, positive in all \CkCapN{} checkpoints (mean \CkCap{}
$[\CkCapLo{},\CkCapHi{}]$) but varying fourfold across them (SD \CkCapSD{}):
general in direction, not in magnitude. The obvious objection is circularity ---
rendering \emph{very} sixteen times really does produce monotonous audio --- but
covarying out realised output diversity leaves the ratio at \CapAdjRatio{} and
restricting to correctly rendered items at \CapCorrRatio{}, on a subset that is
admittedly not like-for-like (\ExactCtl{}\% of controls survive that filter
against \ExactRep{}\%). The gain stays \emph{positive} everywhere: at $k\le32$
repetition slows state acquisition without halting it.

Lemma~\ref{lem:dilution}'s premise holds only approximately ($\delta\le\DeltaMax{}$
nats, S4) and its dose-response prediction fails outright: \emph{within} a
$(\text{model},k)$ cell, items with flatter attention are counted \emph{better},
not worse ($r=\DilR{}$ $[\DilRLo{},\DilRHi{}]$, \DilCells{} cells, all
\DilNAgainst{} measures agreeing; controls at $\DilCtlR{}$; S12). We record it as
disconfirming --- whatever selects which generations fail is not the degree of
dilution --- though a correlational design cannot rule out peaked attention
following from a stalled decoder.
